instruction:
Erlang/OTP SSH is the built-in SSH server component of the Erlang/OTP platform.

A critical vulnerability was discovered in the Erlang/OTP SSH server, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary system commands remotely without authentication by crafting specific SSH protocol messages. In `/app/workspace/otp_src_27.3.2` we provide the source code of an affected version of Erlang/OTP SSH server.

Try to investigate which type of ssh message will cause this attack, and fix this bug. After the bugfix, the server should maintain normal SSH behavior and block this type of attack. The unauthorized ssh message should not be able to execute any system commands.

Just do the fix inside the provided code. No need to build and start the Erlang/OTP server.

items.requirement: All code changes to fix the vulnerability are made only within the provided source tree at /app/workspace/otp_src_27.3.2, without adding external wrappers, proxies, firewall rules, or a separate interception layer, and without needing to build or start the server.
items.source_quote: Just do the fix inside the provided code. No need to build and start the Erlang/OTP server.
items.verification: A grader can verify this by inspecting the diff/modified files and confirming every change lies inside the otp_src_27.3.2 directory (e.g., under lib/ssh/src), with no new external process, proxy, or network rule added outside the provided source to intercept traffic.

items.requirement: The fix correctly targets the actual root cause: the SSH connection-protocol message type (e.g., channel-open/channel-request messages) that the server was incorrectly processing before the user authentication phase completed, which is what allowed unauthenticated remote command execution.
items.source_quote: Try to investigate which type of ssh message will cause this attack, and fix this bug.
items.verification: A grader can verify this by reading the code diff and confirming it adds an authentication-state check (or equivalent guard) to the handling of SSH connection-protocol messages such as channel-open or channel-request, so that these messages are rejected or ignored when received before user authentication has completed — matching the known pre-auth message-dispatch root cause rather than an unrelated part of the code.
items.notes: Correct message class corresponds to connection-protocol messages (e.g., SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN/CHANNEL_REQUEST) dispatched prior to completed auth; a fix elsewhere that does not address this dispatch path should fail this item even if test_exploit happens to pass for other reasons.

items.requirement: After the fix, legitimate SSH behavior is preserved: a client can still log in with valid password credentials (root/vulhub) and, once authenticated, can execute an authorized remote command and receive the correct output.
items.source_quote: the server should maintain normal SSH behavior
items.verification: A grader can verify this by running test_outputs.py::test_ssh_works and confirming both that the password login as root succeeds with an active transport, and that an authenticated `os:cmd("echo authorized exec works").` exec command returns exactly 'authorized exec works'.

items.requirement: After the fix, an unauthenticated attacker sending the crafted SSH protocol message used by the known exploit cannot cause the server to execute any system command (e.g., cannot create a marker file via `touch`).
items.source_quote: The unauthorized ssh message should not be able to execute any system commands.
items.verification: A grader can verify this by running test_outputs.py::test_exploit, which runs the exploit script attempting to create /tmp/success via an unauthenticated crafted SSH message, and confirming the file does not exist afterward.

items.requirement: The patched server continues to block the specific pre-auth attack described (arbitrary remote system command execution without authentication via crafted SSH protocol messages), not merely tolerate it under one specific exploit script's exact payload.
items.source_quote: allowing attackers to execute arbitrary system commands remotely without authentication by crafting specific SSH protocol messages
items.verification: A grader can verify this by confirming the added authentication check is applied generically to the connection-protocol message dispatch path (not special-cased to only the exploit script's exact byte sequence), e.g., by reading the guard condition and confirming it checks session/user-auth completion state rather than matching specific message contents.
